patient.name: Gary Whitfield
patient.setting: Respiratory clinic, then Acute Medical Unit
patient.complaint: Two years of worsening breathlessness, wheeze and morning cough
background: Asthma as a child; hay fever
Smoker, 35 pack-years; still smokes 15 a day
Uses a salbutamol inhaler several times a day

diagnosis.exam: Expect a vignette mixing both diseases: a long-term smoker with childhood asthma or atopy, wheeze and chronic cough, eosinophilia and only partial reversibility. The question is 'most likely diagnosis' or 'most likely spirometry result'.

points: Gary, 56, breathless walking up one flight of stairs.
Wheezy episodes, worse with **cold air and dust**.
Cough with white sputum most mornings for 2 years.

steps.lead: Gary has the asthma picture (variable wheeze, atopy) and the COPD picture (smoker, chronic cough): an **overlap**.
The two risk factors together, **smoking** plus **prior asthma and atopy**, are what make overlap likely.

points: Reduced breath sounds with a widespread expiratory wheeze.

steps.lead: His exam fits the mixed picture. The features that clinch it come next: **eosinophilia** and **partial reversibility**.

steps.q: Which combination best supports overlap rather than pure COPD in Gary?
o: Asthma history, eosinophilia and partial reversibility
steps.r: Hyperinflation, cough and smoking fit COPD alone. **Prior asthma, eosinophilia and partial reversibility** point to overlap.

steps.lead: Without the right inhalers Gary is at risk of **frequent exacerbations** and respiratory failure.

steps.text: Do not call a smoker's wheeze 'just COPD' when there is a **childhood asthma** history and **eosinophilia**. Labelling it COPD may mean he misses the ICS he needs.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely spirometry result?' or 'most appropriate diagnostic investigation': spirometry with reversibility showing FEV1/FVC below 0.7 with partial reversibility, supported by PEF variability and blood eosinophils.

steps.q: Which first tests help most in the clinic?
o: Peak flow variability and blood eosinophils
steps.r: **PEF variability** shows the asthma component; **eosinophils** show eosinophilic inflammation and predict ICS response.

steps.lead: Gary's PEF diary varies by **24%** and his eosinophils are raised: both suggest an asthma component.

visual.title: Gary's blood eosinophils
visual.label: Gary 0.62
visual.caption: Raised eosinophils mark **eosinophilic inflammation** and predict a good ICS response.

steps.title: Spirometry with reversibility
steps.text: FEV1 improves 16%, but the ratio **stays below 0.7**: obstruction that is **partially** reversible.

visual.title: Gary's FEV1/FVC before and after salbutamol
visual.caption: Asthma normalises above 0.7; COPD barely moves; overlap improves but **stays obstructed**.

steps.lead: Gary's post-bronchodilator ratio of **0.58** with a meaningful FEV1 rise is the defining spirometry of overlap.

steps.text: A **post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7** confirms persistent obstruction. Significant reversibility on top of that says there is also an asthma component.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': start ICS early with a long-acting bronchodilator (never LABA alone), escalate to triple therapy, and stop smoking. Exacerbations get controlled oxygen if COPD dominates.

steps.q: Gary uses only salbutamol. Which is the best maintenance inhaler to start?
steps.r: The asthma component needs **ICS**, given early with a long-acting bronchodilator. A LABA without ICS is unsafe in asthma.

steps.lead: Gary starts an **ICS/LABA** inhaler (beclometasone/formoterol) straight away because of his asthma component and eosinophilia.
If Gary stays breathless, bronchodilation is increased: **LABA with or without a LAMA**.
Six months on, still having exacerbations, Gary moves to **triple therapy** (ICS + LABA + LAMA).

steps.title: Gary's treatment pathway
nodes: ICS early with a long-acting bronchodilator
steps.caption: ICS is the base layer in overlap; in pure COPD it is only added for asthmatic features or exacerbations.

steps.lead: The single biggest intervention for Gary is **stopping smoking**; pulmonary rehab improves his exercise tolerance.

points: Winter: Gary arrives at AMU with a 3 day cold and worse wheeze.
Sputum now green; speaking in short sentences.

steps.title: ABG on arrival (on air)
steps.text: Hypoxia with raised pCO2 and a low pH: **acute on chronic type 2 respiratory failure**. COPD is dominant now, so target **88-92%**.

visual.title: Oxygen target for Gary
visual.label: Gary 86% on air
visual.caption: Give controlled oxygen via a **Venturi** mask to reach 88-92%.

steps.lead: Gary gets **controlled oxygen**, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, prednisolone, and antibiotics for his green sputum.
GINA and GOLD guidance on overlap underpins Gary's plan: ICS early, add bronchodilators, treat both diseases.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism: why reversibility is only partial (reversible bronchospasm plus fixed structural damage) and why eosinophilia predicts a good ICS response.

steps.title: Two processes in one airway
steps.caption: Gary has both, which is why salbutamol helps but cannot normalise him.

steps.lead: Gary's childhood asthma gave **eosinophilic** inflammation; 35 years of smoking added **neutrophilic** damage and emphysema.
Salbutamol relaxed his bronchospasm (FEV1 up 16%) but could not undo the **fixed** structural narrowing.

steps.q: Why is Gary likely to respond well to ICS?
steps.r: **Eosinophilic** inflammation is steroid-responsive, like eosinophilic asthma. Neutrophilic COPD inflammation is not.

steps.lead: Gary's eosinophils of **0.62** are why his ICS is expected to cut exacerbations.
With both processes active, Gary's FEV1 falls **faster** than in asthma or COPD alone, so stopping smoking matters even more.

steps.text: Neutrophilic inflammation (COPD) is relatively **steroid-resistant**; eosinophilic inflammation (asthma) is **steroid-sensitive**. That is the logic of eosinophil-guided ICS.

glossary.Asthma-COPD overlap: Persistent airflow obstruction with features of both asthma and COPD.
glossary.COPD: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: persistent, progressive, poorly reversible airflow obstruction, usually from smoking.
glossary.Atopy: Inherited tendency to make IgE to allergens, giving asthma, eczema and hay fever.
glossary.Pack-years: Packs of 20 cigarettes smoked per day multiplied by years smoked.
glossary.Partial reversibility: FEV1 improves significantly after a bronchodilator, but obstruction remains.
glossary.Reversibility: Improvement in FEV1 after a bronchodilator; 12% or more is significant.
glossary.FVC: Forced vital capacity: total volume blown out after a full breath in.
glossary.FEV1/FVC: The ratio of FEV1 to FVC; below 0.7 means obstruction.
glossary.Spirometry: Breathing test measuring FEV1 and FVC to detect obstruction or restriction.
glossary.PEF: Peak expiratory flow, measured with a hand-held meter.
glossary.Hyperinflation: Over-expanded lungs from trapped air, giving a barrel chest and flat diaphragms.
glossary.Eosinophils: White cells driving allergic, steroid-responsive airway inflammation.
glossary.Neutrophilic inflammation: Smoking-driven airway inflammation typical of COPD, relatively steroid-resistant.
glossary.Remodelling: Permanent structural airway change: thickened walls, fibrosis, muscle hypertrophy.
glossary.Emphysema: Permanent destruction of alveolar walls, causing air trapping and poor gas exchange.
glossary.ICS: Inhaled corticosteroid, such as beclometasone or budesonide.
glossary.LABA: Long-acting beta-2 agonist, such as formoterol or salmeterol.
glossary.LAMA: Long-acting muscarinic antagonist, such as tiotropium.
glossary.SABA: Short-acting beta-2 agonist, such as salbutamol.
glossary.Triple therapy: ICS + LABA + LAMA, usually in one inhaler.
glossary.Pulmonary rehabilitation: A supervised exercise and education programme that improves breathlessness and exercise tolerance.
glossary.Type 2 respiratory failure: Low pO2 with a raised pCO2 (above 6.0 kPa).
glossary.Acute on chronic: A sudden worsening on top of a long-standing problem; in blood gases, low pH with raised bicarbonate.
glossary.CO2 retainer: A patient with chronically raised pCO2 who risks worsening with uncontrolled oxygen.
glossary.Venturi mask: A mask that delivers a fixed, controlled oxygen percentage.
glossary.Exacerbation: An acute worsening of symptoms beyond normal day-to-day variation.
glossary.GINA: Global Initiative for Asthma, an international asthma guideline group.
glossary.GOLD: Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease, an international COPD guideline group.
glossary.Th2: T helper 2 cells driving allergic, eosinophilic inflammation.

technique.stem: A 58 year old woman has a 3 year history of breathlessness and wheeze, with cough most mornings. She had asthma as a child and has a 30 pack-year smoking history. Her chest is hyperinflated with widespread wheeze. Blood eosinophils are raised. Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.56, rising to 0.62 after salbutamol, with a 15% rise in FEV1.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.
Childhood asthma plus heavy smoking, eosinophilia, and reversibility that does not normalise the ratio.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Partially reversible obstruction with features of both: **asthma-COPD overlap**.

elim: Asthma alone would normalise the ratio after salbutamol; hers stays below 0.7.
Needs large-volume purulent sputum and often crackles.
Pure COPD shows minimal reversibility and no eosinophilia; she has 15%.
Gives restrictive spirometry and crackles, not wheeze.

steps.x: **B. Asthma-COPD overlap.** Rule: reversibility present but ratio still below 0.7, in a smoker with asthma = overlap.

technique.stem: A 61 year old man who smokes has wheeze, chronic cough and breathlessness. He had asthma as a teenager. His GP suspects a combination of asthma and COPD and wants to confirm persistent obstruction and measure its reversibility.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show for this patient.
The question names exactly what must be measured: obstruction and reversibility.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Spirometry with reversibility**: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 with partial reversibility.

elim: May show hyperinflation but cannot measure obstruction or reversibility.
For pulmonary embolism.
Assesses the heart, not airflow.
Measures gas exchange, not obstruction or its reversibility.

steps.x: **D. Spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility.** Rule: spirometry confirms overlap; partial reversibility separates it from pure COPD.

technique.stem: A 55 year old man has asthma-COPD overlap. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and uses salbutamol only. He has had two exacerbations this year. His blood eosinophil count is 0.5 ×10⁹/L. His pulse rate is 82 bpm, BP 134/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate maintenance inhaler to start?

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now.
Overlap with eosinophilia and exacerbations, on reliever only.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Start **ICS early** with a long-acting bronchodilator (ICS/LABA), plus smoking cessation.

elim: LABA without ICS is unsafe with an asthma component.
Treats the COPD part but leaves eosinophilic inflammation untreated.
An asthma add-on, not first-line in overlap.
Long-term oral steroids are not maintenance therapy.

steps.x: **D. Regular ICS/LABA inhaler.** Rule: overlap = ICS from the start; never LABA alone.

technique.stem: A 60 year old woman with asthma-COPD overlap has spirometry. Her FEV1 rises by 18% after salbutamol, but her FEV1/FVC remains 0.6. She has smoked for 40 years and had asthma since childhood.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her spirometry?
o: Fixed fibrosis of the lung parenchyma
Reversible bronchospasm together with fixed structural airway damage

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to its mechanism.
Part of the obstruction reverses, part does not.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The asthma component reverses; the COPD **structural** component (remodelling, emphysema) is fixed.

elim: Fibrosis gives a restrictive pattern with a normal or high ratio.
Would normalise the ratio, as in asthma.
Gives a flattened flow-volume loop, not this pattern.
Gives a restrictive pattern.

steps.x: **C. Reversible bronchospasm together with fixed structural airway damage.** Rule: partial reversibility = reversible bronchospasm + fixed damage.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has a 2 year history of breathlessness, episodic wheeze and morning cough with white sputum. He had asthma and eczema as a child and has a 32 pack-year smoking history. There is widespread expiratory wheeze. His pulse rate is 84 bpm, BP 136/82 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Childhood asthma and atopy plus a heavy smoking history with mixed symptoms and eosinophilia suggest asthma-COPD overlap.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.

clues: asthma and eczema as a child
steps.x: Atopic asthmatic childhood plus heavy smoking, episodic wheeze plus chronic cough.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A mixed asthma/COPD picture: **asthma-COPD overlap**.

elim: Daily purulent sputum and coarse crackles, not this mixed picture.
Brown plugs, very high IgE and eosinophils, often with bronchiectasis.
Dry cough, fine crackles, clubbing; no wheeze.
Basal emphysema in a younger patient, often with liver disease.

steps.x: **C. Asthma-COPD overlap.** Smoker + prior asthma/atopy + mixed symptoms = overlap.

practice.stem: A 59 year old woman with childhood asthma and a 35 pack-year smoking history has progressive breathlessness and wheeze. Her blood eosinophils are raised. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 140/86 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air.

FEV1/FVC 0.82 with no change after salbutamol
practice.e: Asthma-COPD overlap gives obstruction (FEV1/FVC below 0.7) with partial reversibility; asthma normalises and COPD barely changes.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.
Overlap features: expect obstruction that only partly reverses.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ratio below 0.7 that **improves but stays obstructed**, with significant FEV1 rise.

elim: Normal spirometry; she is obstructed.
Full normalisation suggests asthma alone.
Minimal reversibility suggests pure COPD.
A restrictive pattern.

steps.x: **B. FEV1/FVC 0.55 rising to 0.61, with FEV1 up 15%.** Overlap spirometry: partial reversibility, ratio stays below 0.7.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has COPD diagnosed 5 years ago after 40 pack-years of smoking. He had hay fever and asthma as a child. His symptoms vary from week to week and he has had three exacerbations this year. His pulse rate is 90 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air.

steps.x: A COPD label with atopy, prior asthma and variable symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Polycythaemia reflects chronic hypoxia in COPD.
Lymphopenia is non-specific.
Neutrophilic inflammation is typical of COPD or infection.

steps.x: **E. Raised eosinophil count (0.7 ×10⁹/L).** Eosinophilia in a smoker's obstruction = think overlap.

practice.stem: A 57 year old woman has wheeze, breathlessness and chronic productive cough. Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.58 with a 14% rise in FEV1 after salbutamol. Her blood eosinophils are raised.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

practice.stem: A 66 year old man with asthma-COPD overlap is admitted with an exacerbation. He is drowsy and breathless. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 146/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84% breathing air.

Hypoxia, high pCO2, low pH, raised bicarbonate, drowsiness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute on chronic type 2 respiratory failure**: a complication of overlap exacerbations.

elim: The pH is low; the raised bicarbonate is compensation.

Sudden unilateral pain and reduced breath sounds; not in the stem.
Type 1 has a normal or low pCO2; his is raised.

steps.x: **A. Acute on chronic type 2 respiratory failure.** Raised pCO2 + low pH + high HCO3 = acute on chronic type 2.

practice.stem: A 54 year old woman with asthma since childhood started smoking at 18 and has smoked 20 a day since. Over 5 years her symptoms have become persistent, with daily cough. Despite good adherence to ICS/LABA she has lost more lung function than expected. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her lung function decline?
o: Combined asthma and COPD processes accelerating decline
practice.e: In asthma-COPD overlap, inflammation and remodelling from both processes accelerate lung function decline and exacerbations.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before reading the options.

steps.x: Asthma plus long smoking, progressive persistent symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Overlap: **combined inflammation and remodelling accelerate decline**.

elim: Causes early basal emphysema, usually under 45, often in non-smokers.
Remission would improve, not worsen, lung function.
ICS cause thrush and hoarseness, not falling FEV1.
Does not cause progressive loss of lung function.

steps.x: **C. Combined asthma and COPD processes accelerating decline.** Overlap declines faster than either disease alone.

practice.stem: A 62 year old woman with asthma-COPD overlap takes ICS/LABA with good technique and adherence. She has stopped smoking and completed pulmonary rehabilitation. She still has daily breathlessness and two exacerbations in the past year. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
